lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Hello, do you understand?
lessons.goal: Greet someone politely and say whether you understand English or Hindi

steps.n: Lesson 1. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
This greeting works at any time of day, for hello and goodbye. Listen and repeat, starting from the end of the word.
Once more, say 'hello'.
In India people often say this with their palms pressed together in front of the chest. Now say 'hello'.
Here is the word for the English language. Listen and repeat.
Now, 'you understand', speaking politely to one person. Listen and repeat.
Say 'English'.
The polite word for 'you' is this. Listen and repeat.
Now say 'you understand English'. In Hindi the verb comes at the end: 'you English understand'. Listen and repeat.
To turn that into a question, put a small question word at the front. Listen and repeat.
Ask me if I understand English.
Here is a polite 'no'. The first little word adds respect. Listen and repeat.
And a polite 'yes'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'no'.
Say 'yes'.
Ask me again if I understand English.
Now, 'I understand'. A man says it like this. Listen and repeat.
A woman changes the ending of the verb. Listen, and if you are a woman, repeat this form from now on.
Here is 'I don't understand'. The word for 'not' goes just before the verb. Listen and repeat.
Tell me you understand.
Tell me you don't understand.
Now, 'I don't understand English'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'no, I don't understand English'.

steps.expect: जी नहीं, मैं अंग्रेज़ी नहीं समझता।

steps.t: जी नहीं, मैं अंग्रेज़ी नहीं समझता।
steps.tl: jī nahīn, main angrezī nahīn samajhtā.

steps.n: Say 'hello'.
Here is the word for the Hindi language. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'a little'. Notice the flapped 'r' sound in the middle. Listen and repeat.
Now put it together: 'I understand a little Hindi'. Listen and repeat.
Ask me if I understand English.
Tell me you understand a little Hindi.

steps.q: I'll ask you something in Hindi. Answer that you understand.

steps.n: Notice the word order again: subject, then object, then the verb at the very end. Say 'I don't understand English'.
Tell me you understand a little Hindi.
Now take the first speaker's part. Greet me, then ask if I understand English.

steps.expect: नमस्ते। क्या आप अंग्रेज़ी समझते हैं?

steps.t: नमस्ते। क्या आप अंग्रेज़ी समझते हैं?
steps.tl: namaste. kyā āp angrezī samajhte hain?

steps.n: Now answer: 'no, I don't understand English'.

steps.expect: जी नहीं, मैं अंग्रेज़ी नहीं समझता।

steps.t: जी नहीं, मैं अंग्रेज़ी नहीं समझता।
steps.tl: jī nahīn, main angrezī nahīn samajhtā.

steps.n: Add: 'I understand a little Hindi'.
Listen to the conversation from the beginning once more.

steps.t: नमस्ते। क्या आप अंग्रेज़ी समझते हैं?
steps.tl: namaste. kyā āp angrezī samajhte hain?

steps.t: जी नहीं, मैं अंग्रेज़ी नहीं समझता।
steps.tl: jī nahīn, main angrezī nahīn samajhtā.

steps.n: Well done. In the next lesson you will learn to ask how someone is, say thank you, and say that you speak a little Hindi. This is the end of lesson one.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — How are you? Thank you
lessons.goal: Ask how someone is, answer, thank them, and say you speak a little Hindi

steps.n: Lesson 2. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Say 'hello'.
Ask me if I understand English.
Say 'no, I don't understand English'.

steps.expect: जी नहीं, मैं अंग्रेज़ी नहीं समझता।

steps.t: जी नहीं, मैं अंग्रेज़ी नहीं समझता।
steps.tl: jī nahīn, main angrezī nahīn samajhtā.

steps.n: Tell me you understand a little Hindi.
Now, 'how are you?', said politely. Listen and repeat, from the end.
You already know the first word, the polite 'you'. Now greet me and ask how I am.
Here is the answer, 'I am fine'. The word for fine also means okay or correct. Listen and repeat.
Ask me how I am.
Tell me you are fine.
Here is 'thank you'. It is a formal, Sanskrit-based word. Listen and repeat.
Once more, say 'thank you'.
There is a second, everyday word for thanks, borrowed from Urdu. Both are fine anywhere in India. Listen and repeat.
Listen: 'I am fine, thank you'.
Now you say it.
Now, 'and you?'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I am fine, thank you. And you?'.

steps.expect: मैं ठीक हूँ, धन्यवाद। और आप?

steps.t: मैं ठीक हूँ, धन्यवाद। और आप?
steps.tl: main ṭhīk hūn, dhanyavād. aur āp?

steps.n: Here is 'I am also fine'. The little word for 'also' comes right after 'I'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I am also fine'.
Now, 'Do you speak Hindi?'. Compare 'you speak' with 'you understand', which you know. Listen and repeat.
Ask me if I speak Hindi.
Now, 'I speak a little Hindi'. Listen and repeat.
A woman says it with the feminine ending. Listen, and repeat if that is your form.
Say 'yes, a little'.
Tell me you speak a little Hindi.
Here is 'excuse me', or 'sorry'. You use it to get attention or to apologise. Listen and repeat.
Say 'thank you'.
Say 'excuse me'.
Listen: 'excuse me, do you speak Hindi?'.

steps.t: माफ़ कीजिए, क्या आप हिंदी बोलते हैं?
steps.tl: māf kījiye, kyā āp hindī bolte hain?

steps.n: Now you excuse yourself and ask if I speak Hindi.

steps.expect: माफ़ कीजिए, क्या आप हिंदी बोलते हैं?

steps.t: माफ़ कीजिए, क्या आप हिंदी बोलते हैं?
steps.tl: māf kījiye, kyā āp hindī bolte hain?

steps.n: Here is 'please'. Hindi speakers use it less than English speakers do; politeness usually sits in the verb ending instead. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I am also fine'.
Here is a friendly goodbye, 'we'll meet again'. Listen and repeat.

steps.q: Someone asks you how you are. Answer that you are fine and thank them.

steps.n: Say 'see you again'.
Say 'thanks', the everyday way.
Now you take both parts of the conversation. Greet me and ask how I am.
Answer: 'I am fine, thank you. And you?'.

steps.expect: मैं ठीक हूँ, धन्यवाद। और आप?

steps.t: मैं ठीक हूँ, धन्यवाद। और आप?
steps.tl: main ṭhīk hūn, dhanyavād. aur āp?

steps.n: Say 'I am also fine. Do you speak Hindi?'.

steps.expect: मैं भी ठीक हूँ। क्या आप हिंदी बोलते हैं?

steps.t: मैं भी ठीक हूँ। क्या आप हिंदी बोलते हैं?
steps.tl: main bhī ṭhīk hūn. kyā āp hindī bolte hain?

steps.n: Answer: 'yes, a little'.
And say goodbye: 'see you again'.
Listen to the whole conversation once more.

steps.t: मैं ठीक हूँ, धन्यवाद। और आप?
steps.tl: main ṭhīk hūn, dhanyavād. aur āp?

steps.t: मैं भी ठीक हूँ। क्या आप हिंदी बोलते हैं?
steps.tl: main bhī ṭhīk hūn. kyā āp hindī bolte hain?

steps.n: Very good. Next time you will learn to ask where something is, ask how much it costs, and count from one to ten. This is the end of lesson two.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Where is it? How much?
lessons.goal: Ask where something is, ask prices, and count from one to ten

steps.n: Lesson 3. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Say 'excuse me'.
Say 'I am fine, thank you. And you?'.

steps.expect: मैं ठीक हूँ, धन्यवाद। और आप?

steps.t: मैं ठीक हूँ, धन्यवाद। और आप?
steps.tl: main ṭhīk hūn, dhanyavād. aur āp?

steps.n: Ask me if I speak Hindi.
Here is 'where is?'. The word for 'is' comes last, as always. Listen and repeat.
The word for station is borrowed from English. Listen and repeat.
Now, 'where is the station?'. The thing you are looking for comes first. Listen and repeat.
Excuse yourself and ask where the station is.
Here is the answer 'it is there'. Listen and repeat.
And 'here'. Notice how close the two words sound. Listen and repeat.
Say 'the station is there'.
Here is 'hotel'. Listen and repeat.
Ask where the hotel is.
And a very useful word: 'bathroom'. Listen and repeat.
Ask where the bathroom is.
Now the numbers from one to ten. Listen and repeat each one.
Again: one, two, three.
Four, five, six.
Seven, eight, nine, ten.
Now count from one to ten on your own.

steps.t: एक, दो, तीन, चार, पाँच, छह, सात, आठ, नौ, दस
steps.tl: ek, do, tīn, chār, pānch, chhah, sāt, āṭh, nau, das

steps.n: Say 'three'.
Say 'ten'.
Ask where the station is.
Here is 'how much is it?', literally 'of how much is it'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'this'. Listen and repeat.
Now, 'how much is this?'.
Here is the Indian currency, 'rupees'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'ten rupees'.
Ask how much this is.
Answer: 'five rupees'.
Here is 'very expensive'. In many Indian markets a polite 'very expensive' opens a friendly bargain. Listen and repeat.
Say 'very expensive'.
Ask where the bathroom is.
Say 'how much is this?'.
Now take the traveller's part. Excuse yourself and ask where the station is.
Answer: 'the station is there'.
Say 'thank you. And how much is this?'.

steps.expect: धन्यवाद। और यह कितने का है?

steps.t: धन्यवाद। और यह कितने का है?
steps.tl: dhanyavād. aur yah kitne kā hai?

steps.n: Answer: 'ten rupees'.
Listen to the conversation once more.

steps.t: धन्यवाद। और यह कितने का है?
steps.tl: dhanyavād. aur yah kitne kā hai?

steps.n: Excellent. In the next lesson you will order tea and food, and learn to say what you would like. This is the end of lesson three.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Tea, water and food
lessons.goal: Order drinks and food, say what you would like, and ask for the bill

steps.n: Lesson 4. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Say 'how much is this?'.
Say 'ten rupees'.
Here is 'tea'. In India it is usually boiled with milk and sugar. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'please give'. The ending makes it polite, like 'excuse me', which ends the same way. Listen and repeat.
Now, 'please give one tea'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'water'. Listen and repeat.
Ask for water: 'please give water'.
Here is 'sugar'. Listen and repeat.
And 'without sugar'. Listen and repeat.
Order one tea without sugar.
Here is 'I would like', literally 'to me is needed'. The first word means 'to me'. Listen and repeat.
Now, 'I would like water'. The thing you want goes in the middle. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I would like tea'.
Here is what a shopkeeper asks: 'what would you like?'. Listen and repeat.
You heard the shopkeeper add a little word after the greeting. It is a respectful tag you can add to names and to yes and no. Listen.
Ask me what I would like.
Answer: 'I would like water'.
Here is 'coffee'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'anything else?', literally 'more something?'. Listen and repeat.
Ask me 'anything else?'.
Answer: 'yes, water too'.
Here is 'food', which is also the verb 'to eat'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I would like food'.
Two common dishes. First, the everyday flatbread. Listen and repeat.
And lentil curry, eaten almost every day across India. Listen and repeat.
Order lentils and flatbread: 'please give lentils and flatbread'.
To compliment the cook, say 'it is very tasty'. Listen and repeat.
Tell me the food is very tasty.
Here is 'bill'. Listen and repeat.
Ask for the bill.
Order one tea without sugar.
Ask how much this is.
Now take the customer's part. I am the tea seller.
Order one tea without sugar.
Answer: 'yes, water too. Thank you'.
Listen to the conversation once more.
Well done. Next time you will ask for directions and take an auto-rickshaw. This is the end of lesson four.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — How far? Go straight
lessons.goal: Ask how far a place is, follow simple directions, and bargain for an auto

steps.n: Lesson 5. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Ask where the station is.
Say 'I would like water'.
In north India you call a man you don't know 'brother sir'. It is friendly and respectful. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'airport', borrowed from English. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'how far is it?'. The word for 'far' is in the middle. Listen and repeat.
Now, 'how far is the airport?'. Listen and repeat.
Get a man's attention and ask how far the airport is.

steps.expect: भाई साहब, एयरपोर्ट कितनी दूर है?

steps.t: भाई साहब, एयरपोर्ट कितनी दूर है?
steps.tl: bhāī sāhab, eyarporṭ kitnī dūr hai?

steps.n: Ask how far the station is.
Here is the answer 'not very far'. The first word means 'more' or 'too much'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'not very far'.
Now, 'go straight', said politely. The verb ending is the same polite one as in 'please give'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'left'. Listen and repeat.
And 'right'. Listen and repeat.
Tell me to go straight.
You know 'again' from 'see you again'; it also means 'then'. Say 'go straight, then left'.
Say 'go straight, then right'.
Here is the three-wheeled auto-rickshaw, simply called 'auto'. Listen and repeat.
And 'taxi'. Listen and repeat.
Now, 'how much will it be by auto?'. The little word after 'auto' means 'by' or 'from'. Listen and repeat.
Ask how much it will be by taxi.
Ask how far the airport is.
Here is 'one hundred'. Listen and repeat.
'Two hundred'.
'Five hundred'.
Say 'two hundred rupees'.
Say 'very expensive'.
Ask how much it will be by auto.
When you reach your stop, say 'stop here'. Listen and repeat.
Tell the driver to stop here.
Many auto drivers do not use the meter, so agree the fare before you get in. Ask 'how much will it be by auto?', then say 'very expensive'.

steps.q: The driver says the airport is not very far. Repeat what he said.

steps.n: Say 'go straight, then left'.
Say 'thank you, brother'.
Now take the traveller's part. Get the shopkeeper's attention and ask how far the airport is.

steps.expect: भाई साहब, एयरपोर्ट कितनी दूर है?

steps.t: भाई साहब, एयरपोर्ट कितनी दूर है?
steps.tl: bhāī sāhab, eyarporṭ kitnī dūr hai?

steps.t: ज़्यादा दूर नहीं। सीधे जाइए, फिर बाएँ।
steps.tl: zyādā dūr nahīn. sīdhe jāiye, phir bāyen.

steps.n: Ask how much it will be by auto.
Say 'very expensive'.
Listen to the conversation once more.

steps.t: भाई साहब, एयरपोर्ट कितनी दूर है?
steps.tl: bhāī sāhab, eyarporṭ kitnī dūr hai?

steps.t: ज़्यादा दूर नहीं। सीधे जाइए, फिर बाएँ।
steps.tl: zyādā dūr nahīn. sīdhe jāiye, phir bāyen.

steps.n: Very good. In the next lesson you will ask the time and learn the days of the week. This is the end of lesson five.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — What time is it?
lessons.goal: Ask and tell the time, say today and tomorrow, and name the days of the week

steps.n: Lesson 6. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Ask how much it will be by auto.
Say 'two hundred rupees'.
Count from one to ten.

steps.expect: एक, दो, तीन, चार, पाँच, छह, सात, आठ, नौ, दस

steps.t: एक, दो, तीन, चार, पाँच, छह, सात, आठ, नौ, दस
steps.tl: ek, do, tīn, chār, pānch, chhah, sāt, āṭh, nau, das

steps.n: Here is 'what time is it?', literally 'how many o'clock are there?'. Listen and repeat.
The answer uses the same pattern: 'it is three o'clock'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'it is five o'clock'.
One o'clock is special: it is singular, so the ending changes. Listen and repeat.
Excuse yourself and ask what time it is.
Answer: 'it is three o'clock'.
Here is 'today'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'tomorrow'. The same word also means 'yesterday'; the verb tense tells you which. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'morning'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'evening'. Listen and repeat.
And 'night'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'tomorrow morning'.
To say 'in the evening', you add a small word after 'evening'. Here is 'this evening'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'tomorrow evening'.
Say 'it is one o'clock'.
Now the days of the week. Most end in the word for 'day'. Listen and repeat each one. Monday.
Tuesday.
Wednesday.
Thursday.
Friday.
Saturday.
Sunday.
Listen to the whole week, then say it yourself.

steps.t: सोमवार, मंगलवार, बुधवार, गुरुवार, शुक्रवार, शनिवार, रविवार
steps.tl: somvār, mangalvār, budhvār, guruvār, shukravār, shanivār, ravivār

steps.n: Here is 'what day is it today?', literally 'today which day is?'. Listen and repeat.
Answer: 'today is Monday'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'today is Friday'.
Say 'tomorrow is Tuesday'.
Ask what day it is today.
Here is 'now'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'now it is three o'clock'.
Many Indians use an older form for Thursday and Sunday too. Listen, so you recognise them.

steps.q: I will ask you the time. Answer that it is seven o'clock.

steps.n: Say 'today is Monday'.
Now take the first speaker's part. Excuse yourself and ask the time.
Ask 'and what day is it today?'.

steps.expect: और आज कौन सा दिन है?

steps.t: और आज कौन सा दिन है?
steps.tl: aur āj kaun sā din hai?

steps.n: Now answer: 'today is Monday. Tomorrow Tuesday'.
Listen to the conversation once more.

steps.t: और आज कौन सा दिन है?
steps.tl: aur āj kaun sā din hai?

steps.n: Well done. In the next lesson you will introduce yourself and talk about your family. This is the end of lesson six.

lessons.title: Lesson 7 — My name is… This is my family
lessons.goal: Introduce yourself, say where you are from, and introduce family members

steps.n: Lesson 7. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Say 'hello, how are you?'.
Tell me you speak a little Hindi.
Here is 'name'. Listen and repeat.
Now, 'my name is Rahul'. Listen and repeat.
Now say it with your own name.
Here is 'what is your name?'. The word for 'your' is built from the polite 'you'. Listen and repeat.
Ask me my name.
Say 'my name is Rahul'.
Here is 'where are you from?'. You know 'where' and the little word for 'from'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'I am from America'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I am from Delhi'.
Ask me where I am from.
Answer: 'I am from America'.
Here is 'this is my wife'. Notice 'my' now ends in a long 'ee', because wife is feminine. Listen and repeat.
And 'this is my husband'. For respect, a husband takes the plural form, so 'my' and 'is' both change. Listen and repeat.
Introduce your wife.
Introduce your husband.
Here is 'son'. Listen and repeat.
And 'daughter'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'this is my son'.
Say 'this is my daughter'.
So: masculine nouns take 'my' with an 'aa' sound, feminine nouns with an 'ee' sound, and respected elders take the plural form. Ask me my name.
Here is 'mother'. Listen and repeat.
And 'father'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'this is my mother'.
Say 'this is my father'.
Here is 'brother'. Listen and repeat.
And 'sister'.
Say 'this is my brother'.
Say 'this is my sister'.
Here is 'pleased to meet you', literally 'having met you, happiness happened'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'pleased to meet you'.

steps.q: Someone asks where you are from. Answer that you are from America.

steps.n: Introduce your daughter.
Now take Rahul's part. Greet her, say your name is Rahul, and ask her name.

steps.expect: नमस्ते, मेरा नाम राहुल है। आपका नाम क्या है?

steps.t: नमस्ते, मेरा नाम राहुल है। आपका नाम क्या है?
steps.tl: namaste, merā nām rāhul hai. āpkā nām kyā hai?

steps.t: मेरा नाम अना है। आप कहाँ से हैं?
steps.tl: merā nām anā hai. āp kahān se hain?

steps.n: Say 'I am from Delhi. This is my wife'.

steps.expect: मैं दिल्ली से हूँ। यह मेरी पत्नी है।

steps.t: मैं दिल्ली से हूँ। यह मेरी पत्नी है।
steps.tl: main dillī se hūn. yah merī patnī hai.

steps.n: Now take Ana's part: 'pleased to meet you'.
Listen to the conversation once more.

steps.t: नमस्ते, मेरा नाम राहुल है। आपका नाम क्या है?
steps.tl: namaste, merā nām rāhul hai. āpkā nām kyā hai?

steps.t: मेरा नाम अना है। आप कहाँ से हैं?
steps.tl: merā nām anā hai. āp kahān se hain?

steps.t: मैं दिल्ली से हूँ। यह मेरी पत्नी है।
steps.tl: main dillī se hūn. yah merī patnī hai.

steps.n: Excellent. Next time you will say what you like and what you want to do. This is the end of lesson seven.

lessons.title: Lesson 8 — I like it, I want to go
lessons.goal: Say what you like and dislike, and what you want or want to do

steps.n: Lesson 8. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Say 'I would like tea'.
Ask me where I am from.
Here is 'I like', literally 'to me it is pleasing'. You know the first word from 'I would like'. Listen and repeat.
Now, 'I like tea'. The thing you like goes in the middle, just like before. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'Indian'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I like Indian food'.
Here is 'to you', the partner of 'to me'. Listen and repeat.
Now, 'do you like Indian food?'. Listen and repeat.

steps.t: क्या आपको भारतीय खाना पसंद है?
steps.tl: kyā āpko bhāratīya khānā pasand hai?

steps.t: क्या आपको भारतीय खाना पसंद है?
steps.tl: kyā āpko bhāratīya khānā pasand hai?

steps.expect: क्या आपको भारतीय खाना पसंद है?

steps.t: क्या आपको भारतीय खाना पसंद है?
steps.tl: kyā āpko bhāratīya khānā pasand hai?

steps.expect: क्या आपको भारतीय खाना पसंद है?

steps.n: Ask me if I like tea.

steps.t: जी हाँ, मुझे बहुत पसंद है
steps.tl: jī hān, mujhe bahut pasand hai

steps.n: Answer: 'yes, I like it a lot'.

steps.expect: जी हाँ, मुझे बहुत पसंद है

steps.t: जी हाँ, मुझे बहुत पसंद है
steps.tl: jī hān, mujhe bahut pasand hai

steps.n: Here is 'I don't like coffee'. Notice that 'not' slips in just before 'is'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'music'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I like music'.
Say 'I don't like coffee'.
Here is 'especially'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'especially lentils'.
Here is 'do you want tea?'. This is the verb 'to want', related to 'I would like'. Listen and repeat.
And 'I want coffee', a man speaking. Listen and repeat.
A woman says it like this. Repeat if that is your form.

steps.n: Here is 'I went to the market', a man speaking. The past form of 'go' comes at the end. Listen and repeat.

Here is 'where did you go?'. With the polite 'you', the verb takes a plural ending. Listen and repeat.
You know the word for tomorrow. With a past verb it means 'yesterday'. Ask 'where did you go yesterday?'.
Answer: 'I went to the market'.
Say 'yesterday I went to Delhi'.
Here is 'I ate food'. In the past tense, verbs that take an object use a special form of 'I', with an extra syllable. Listen and repeat.
That special form appears only in the past with verbs like eat, drink or see, never with 'go'. Say 'I ate food'.
Here is 'I drank tea'. The verb agrees with 'tea', which is feminine, so it ends in a long 'ee'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I went to the market. I drank tea'.
